briefing.text: Do not let a Fisher or hypergeometric p-value decide the verdict on BRAF/KRAS mutual exclusivity. KRAS is mutated in about 90% of PDA and BRAF in about 1-3%, so a cohort of about 100 samples has almost no power, and a non-significant test is not evidence against exclusivity. What decides it is two sample counts: how many samples carry both oncogenic KRAS and oncogenic BRAF, and how many oncogenic-BRAF samples are KRAS wild-type. For any sample that carries both, check whether it is hypermutated, because an overlap in a non-hypermutated tumour is real evidence against exclusivity.
briefing.reason: A team that reads an underpowered, non-significant p-value as a verdict will get the label wrong. This sets the decision rule.

briefing.text: Define 'oncogenic' before you count, and count samples, not variants. Build one row per sample (Tumor_Sample_Barcode) from data_mutations.txt. Keep only protein-altering classes: Missense, In_Frame_Del/Ins, Nonsense, Frame_Shift, Splice_Site. Drop Silent, intronic, UTR, flank and splice_region rows. Call a sample KRAS-mutant only if it has a hotspot at codon 12, 13 or 61 (also 117 or 146). Take the denominator from all sequenced samples in data_gene_panel_matrix.txt, including samples with no mutation rows. For every BRAF-mutant sample, list HGVSp_Short and Variant_Classification next to that sample's KRAS status.
briefing.reason: Counting non-functional calls, duplicate rows or non-hotspot KRAS changes can create overlaps that are not real, or give the wrong denominator.

briefing.text: Put each BRAF variant into a class before you judge any overlap. Class 1 is V600E/K/D/R. Class 2 is RAS-independent dimers: K601E, L597, G464/G469, the in-frame beta3-alphaC deletions such as N486_P490del and V487_P492delinsA, and fusions. Class 3 is kinase-impaired and RAS-dependent, such as D594G/N, G466V and N581S. Anything else is a VUS. Class 1 and 2 BRAF is expected to be exclusive with KRAS. Class 3 BRAF often co-occurs with RAS mutations, and passenger or VUS BRAF changes in a KRAS-mutant tumour do not break exclusivity. Cross-tabulate BRAF class against KRAS status, and report class 3 or VUS overlaps separately from overlaps involving class 1 or 2. Overlap with V600E or with an in-frame deletion counts against the hypothesis. These classes come from domain knowledge (Yao et al. 2017; Yaeger & Corcoran 2019; OncoKB) and were not checked against fetched sources.
briefing.reason: Whether a BRAF/KRAS overlap counts against the hypothesis depends on which BRAF variant is involved. Without this, a team could misread a class 3 or VUS co-occurrence.

briefing.text: The hypothesis is about mutations, so base the main exclusivity 2x2 table on data_mutations.txt only. A BRAF copy-number gain in data_cna.txt is not an oncogenic BRAF mutation, and GISTIC +1/+2 calls in low-purity PDA are noisy. Look at BRAF CNA only as a secondary observation, and do not count a BRAF gain in a KRAS-mutant tumour as a break in exclusivity.
briefing.reason: The dataset includes CNA files. Mixing amplifications into the test could create overlaps that are not real.

briefing.text: This dataset is a whole-exome PDA (PAAD) cohort from UT Southwestern. The hypothesis names the same cancer type and the same genes, which matters when you apply the benchmark's rule for telling 'Not verifiable' apart from 'True'/'False'.
briefing.reason: Under the labelling convention, the first decision is whether the hypothesis is about this study, so the teams need to know what the cohort is.

shared_assumptions: Both teams treat 'mutually exclusive' as 'zero co-mutated samples observed' and accept 3 BRAF-mutant samples as enough. Neither asked whether, with a ~92% KRAS-mutant rate, zero overlap is also what independence would predict for so few BRAF mutants.
Both assume a KRAS wild-type call from WXS is a true negative, although allele counts are missing for KRAS/BRAF rows and low-cellularity PDA commonly hides KRAS mutations.

Both define oncogenic BRAF from point mutations only. Neither reports looking for BRAF in-frame deletions (beta3-alphaC) or fusions, the other recurrent BRAF events in KRAS-wild-type PDA, though In_Frame_Del rows exist in the file.
unused_evidence: Validation_Status column: 36 KRAS/BRAF rows are 'Valid' and the rest blank. Neither team used it to say which BRAF and KRAS calls were orthogonally validated.
data_cna_hg19.seg was not used to judge tumour purity of the KRAS-wild-type samples or to look for BRAF rearrangement breakpoints.
Clinical columns (stage, nodal status, radiation therapy) were not used to check whether the cohort is a selected subgroup.

Other RAS/MAPK genes (NRAS, HRAS, NF1, MAP2K1, ERBB2) in KRAS-wild-type samples were not examined. A recurrent identical NF1 frameshift across several samples also suggests that artefact calls exist in this MAF.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A named possible KRAS false negatives (VAF unavailable) but only reported it and did not resolve it.
Team B named the n=3 BRAF group as its weakest point and relied on its Fisher p without testing purity or call quality of the 9 KRAS-wild-type samples.
second_readings: 'Oncogenic BRAF mutations' could mean all BRAF alterations or only activating classes (V600, in-frame deletions, fusions). All observed are V600E, so both readings agree unless non-missense BRAF events were missed.

'Mutually exclusive' could be descriptive (zero overlap) or statistical (significant anti-co-occurrence). The hypothesis concerns this PDA study, so under the convention the label is True/False, not Not verifiable.
challenge.verdict: I trust the agreed 'True' fairly well: the hypothesis is about this PDA cohort, all 3 BRAF V600E samples are KRAS wild-type, and this matches established biology. The open risks are KRAS false negatives in low-purity samples and unchecked non-point-mutation BRAF events, and neither is likely to flip the label.

findings.question: In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, which classes of BRAF alteration (V600 missense, beta3-alphaC in-frame deletions, fusions, class III kinase-impaired mutations) are reported to be mutually exclusive with, or to co-occur with, KRAS mutations?
findings.answer: NOT SETTLED BY THE WEB: the research gateway returned HTTP 403 on every call (4 attempts), so I read no pages. From domain knowledge only (unverified): in PDAC, BRAF V600E (class I), beta3-alphaC in-frame deletions such as N486_P490del (class II) and BRAF fusions are reported almost only in KRAS-wild-type tumours, so they behave as mutually exclusive alternative MAPK drivers. Class III kinase-impaired mutations such as D594G and G466V depend on RAS and can co-occur with KRAS. For the claim, 'oncogenic BRAF' should mean class I/II and fusions. Overlap involving only class III mutations or variants of unknown significance does not refute exclusivity.

findings.question: How do mutual-exclusivity tests (Fisher exact, DISCOVER, CoMEt) behave when one gene is altered in over 90% of samples, and is the Fisher p-value biased under heterogeneous per-sample mutation rates?
findings.answer: NOT SETTLED BY THE WEB: the gateway returned HTTP 403 and I read no pages. From domain knowledge only (unverified): when one gene is altered in over 90% of samples and the other in about 1-3%, there are very few KRAS-wild-type samples. So Fisher, DISCOVER and CoMEt all have almost no power, and even zero overlap usually gives a non-significant p-value. The Fisher exact test assumes every sample has the same chance of alteration. When mutation rates differ between samples, hypermutated tumours tend to carry both genes, which makes Fisher conservative, biased against detecting exclusivity. DISCOVER (Canisius et al. 2016) and weighted tests such as WExT were built to correct this. A non-significant Fisher p-value is therefore weak evidence either way. Direct counts of the overlap, with hypermutated samples flagged, are more informative.
